description: Beyond.eg is a team of engineers and innovators passionate about technology, space, and solving real-world challenges. We combine programming, engineering, and creativity to build impactful solutions. We welcome members skilled in AI, software, data, design, and research to collaborate with us.
summary:
STELLAR is a working prototype that gives every astronaut a personal digital twin. During the first 14 mission days it learns each crew member's own normal heart rate, HRV, SpO2, temperature, sleep and activity. It then fuses wearable, suit and camera data, scores health risk from 0 to 100 with a machine-learning model, and explains every alert in plain language, such as "Blood oxygen is 4.6 points below your normal."
Why it matters: in space the body's "normal" changes, so fixed Earth thresholds fail. In our simulated mission, Omar's heart rate never crossed 100 bpm and a standard alarm stayed silent, yet STELLAR flagged him 10 hours before his emergency, with zero false alarms for a healthy crewmate. With Mars communication delays of up to 22 minutes, decisions must happen next to the astronaut: STELLAR runs fully offline at the edge, and when the link to Earth drops, emergency messages are sent first.
It also replays real NASA space weather (OMNIWeb, DONKI): a real solar radiation storm triggers a shelter alert. We built a FastAPI backend, a live Ground Control dashboard and a one-click demo. Crew data is synthetic; outputs are monitoring indicators, not diagnoses.
details:
STELLAR flagged an astronaut 10 hours before his emergency, even though his heart rate never crossed 100 bpm and a standard alarm stayed silent. (Result from our simulated 60-day mission.)

What it does

STELLAR is a health-monitoring system for astronauts built around one idea: every person has their own “normal”. Instead of comparing a crew member with population thresholds made on Earth, it learns that astronaut’s personal baseline and watches for changes against it.

How it works

  • Digital twin (personal baseline). During the first 14 mission days, the system learns each astronaut’s normal heart rate, heart-rate variability, blood oxygen, skin temperature, respiration, sleep and activity, using a robust median-based range that a few bad readings cannot distort.
  • Data fusion. Every hour, wearable data, suit and cabin telemetry (pressure, temperature, oxygen, CO2) and camera features from body pose (posture, movement quality, fatigue during exercise) are fused into one health vector, together with features from the last 7 days. Fusion also rates fatigue as Low, Medium or High and flags cabin values outside safe limits.
  • Risk prediction. A hybrid model (Random Forest classifier, Isolation Forest anomaly detector and clinical early-warning points) produces a risk score from 0 to 100 and one of four levels: Normal, Attention, High Risk, Emergency.
  • Explanation. Every score comes with reasons in plain language, such as “Blood oxygen is 4.6 points below your normal”, plus a recommendation.
  • Alerts and communication. High Risk and Emergency create alerts, with emergencies always shown first. A simulated space-to-ground link queues data by priority: when the link drops and returns, emergency messages are delivered before everything else.
  • Space weather from NASA data. Mission days 1-60 replay the real space weather of 25 August - 23 October 2024 (solar maximum): hourly Kp and Dst from NASA OMNIWeb, and radiation and geomagnetic storms from NASA DONKI. When the real 9 October 2024 radiation storm (>100 MeV protons at Earth orbit) arrives, STELLAR sends a crew-wide alert: move to the shielded area and postpone spacewalks. Radiation is one of NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight.
  • Ground Control dashboard. One screen shows the whole crew, the selected astronaut’s score, reasons, personal normal ranges, suit and camera data with the fatigue level, NASA space weather, a risk chart, alerts with an Acknowledge button, and the link status.

Benefits

  • Earlier warnings: a High Risk warning 10 hours before the emergency, where a fixed alarm stayed silent.
  • Fewer false alarms: a healthy crewmate stayed Normal for the entire run.
  • Trust: crew and doctors see why a score changed, in plain language, not just a number.
  • Works without Earth: everything runs offline on one laptop, which matters when a message to Mars can take up to about 22 minutes one way.

Intended impact

Support crew autonomy on long missions to the Moon and Mars, where real-time help from Earth is not possible. The same approach can serve people on Earth who are far from a doctor: remote workers, polar stations and rural patients with wearables.

Tools and technologies

Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn, MediaPipe Pose and OpenCV (camera analysis), PostgreSQL (SQLite offline fallback), Docker, JWT with role-based access, a single-page HTML/JavaScript dashboard, real NASA data (OMNIWeb and DONKI API), and 223 automated tests. Hardware: one ordinary laptop.

What makes it creative

  • A personal “normal” for each astronaut instead of one threshold for everyone.
  • Plain-language explanations that say what changed and by how much.
  • Built for the distance problem: decisions are made next to the astronaut, and Earth receives the most important information first.
  • Real NASA space weather inside the system: the real 9 October 2024 radiation storm sends the crew to shelter on mission day 46.
  • A 60-day mission replay that tells the whole story live in a few minutes.

Factors the team considered

  • Safety: outputs are monitoring indicators, never a diagnosis. The doctor and crew decide.
  • False alarms: alerts are de-duplicated and levels are calibrated to avoid alert fatigue.
  • Reliability: if an AI component fails, a simple backup model takes over and the error is logged, so monitoring never stops.
  • Security and privacy: role-based login, each astronaut sees only their own data, login lockout, a security event log, and the model file is loaded with an allow-list so a tampered file is refused.
  • Honesty about data: the space weather is real NASA data. The crew data is synthetic, generated from ranges reported in NASA and scientific sources, and in the demo the suit telemetry and daily camera check are simulated too. Real-world accuracy still needs real data.
